newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb defiance won't affect aid - official.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb defiance won't affect aid - official.

text.p: Reconstruction aid would go on flowing into Bosnian Serb territory despite the refusal of its leadership to extradite indicted war criminals, an international official said in Sarajevo on Friday.

Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic made clear last week in a letter to Kofi Annan, the new United Nations secretary general, that authorities would not hand over wartime political and military leaders charged by a U.N. war crimes tribunal.

The letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, warned that the arrest of suspects such as former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic or army chief Ratko Mladic would cause "massive civil and military unrest".

Colum Murphy, spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, criticised the letter on Friday but said it would not prevent the country's Serb republic from receiving post-war economic aid.
"It makes no difference as I would see it on the flow of reconstruction aid being discussed in Brussels at the moment," he told reporters in Sarajevo.
Murphy was referring to a conference in Brussels where envoys from Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat territories met donors this week to appeal for more financial aid to rebuild the shattered country.
"The letter contains a number of legal arguments and all that is proper and appropriate even if one disagrees with the arguments made," he said.
"What we seek is the rule of law and we much prefer that people make legal arguments than solve problems out of a barrel of a gun."
The reaction from the High Representative's office appeared to contradict conclusions from an international conference on Bosnia last month.
Major powers attending the London summit on the Bosnia peace process had warned that reconstruction aid would be "closely linked" to cooperation with the U.N. tribunal.
The conference vowed to "increase pressure" on authorities in former Yugoslavia which have failed to extradite those indicted by the tribunal.

The autonomous Serb republic has received only about two percent of all reconstruction aid given to Bosnia so far because its leadership refused to attend a donors' conference last year as part of a single Bosnia delegation.
This year, the Serbs agreed to travel to the conference as part of united delegation representing Bosnia.
Murphy said Plavsic's arguments about refusing to cooperate with the tribunal were "specious, disingenuous and in our opinion quite wrong".
"The office of the High Representative has always rejected the argument that indicted war criminals should not be arrested simply because it would cause civil unrest.
"There might some temporary upheaval but we have always felt that the pursuit of justice was worth it," he said.
A Sarajevo spokesman for the United Nations and the war crimes tribunal confirmed the letter's contents but declined to comment further.
